args.text: [lane-otter] Three risks of caching Domain Name System (DNS) answers for too long: (1) Stale answers: users are sent to an old server address after a site moves or fails over, causing outages. (2) Slow security response: if a bad or hijacked answer is cached, it keeps being served long after the fix. (3) Hampered change and recovery: planned migrations and emergency switches take far longer to reach everyone, and the delay is unknown in advance because each resolver caches separately.

[lane-otter] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If the request is idempotent, meaning repeating it gives the same result as doing it once, a retry cannot cause harm such as charging a customer twice.

[lane-otter] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier whose first part is a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Leaked timing: the ID reveals roughly when a row was created, so it can expose activity patterns or let others guess record ages. (2) Size and ordering limits: it takes 16 bytes, larger than a plain integer key, so indexes grow bigger; and IDs made at the same moment on different servers are only roughly ordered, not strictly.

[lane-otter] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a file where a database records each change before applying it to the main data files. If the system crashes, it replays the log to recover committed changes and discard unfinished ones, so no data is lost or left half-written.

[lane-otter] (1) Reproducibility: the same client version means anyone rerunning the benchmark gets comparable results, because performance and behaviour can change between releases. (2) Fair comparison: if the client changes mid-study, you cannot tell whether a difference came from the system under test or from the new client, so pinning isolates the variable you actually want to measure.

[lane-otter] Backpressure is a way for a queue to tell the things feeding it to slow down when the consumers cannot keep up, for example by blocking the sender, rejecting new items or signalling it to pause. This stops the queue growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory and make delays worse for everyone.

[lane-otter] A cron job can run twice when (1) the same schedule is installed on two machines or in two places, such as a duplicated crontab entry or two servers behind a load balancer, and (2) a run is slow and the next scheduled run starts before it finishes, so the two overlap. One guard is a lock, for example a file lock taken with flock or a database advisory lock, so a second run exits at once if the first still holds it.

[lane-otter] A tombstone is a small marker that records that an item has been deleted, instead of removing the item straight away. In a replicated store it is needed because a copy that missed the delete would otherwise send the old item back to the others; the marker tells every copy the item is gone, and it is only cleaned up after all copies have seen it.

[lane-otter] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change in between, for example when you simply run it again; (2) its result depends on things outside the code, such as timing, the order tests run in, or a shared resource, so it fails only now and then. A test that truly fails does so every time.

[lane-otter] A lease-based lock gives a client the lock only until a set expiry time. If clocks disagree, a client with a slow clock may think its lease is still valid after the lock service has already given it to someone else, so two clients act at once. A fast clock can also make a lease seem to end early, so work is dropped or repeated.
